title: Closed Form for the k=3 Birthday Count at n = 4
description: Extends the parent's closed forms for the slot recurrence R (k=3 birthday counting, at most two people per day) to n = 4: the number of ways to seat four labelled people on d days with at most two per day equals d⁴ − 4d² + 3d, equivalently d(d−1)(d²+d−3). The parent gave the closed forms for n = 1, 2, 3 (the last being d³ − d); this is the next term. Stated over ℤ to avoid truncated subtraction, and proved by directly unfolding the recurrence — no native_decide — so it is fully 0-axiom, unlike several of the parent's tabulated threshold values.

meta.author: Lean Genius
meta.assumptions: None. #print axioms reports only propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound. The closed form is proved by unfolding the recurrence (no native_decide), so it carries no Lean.ofReduceBool dependency.

birthdayCount3_four_eq_nat: a clean ℕ identity (birthdayCount3 4 d + 4d² = d⁴ + 3d) valid for d ≥ 1

mainTheorems.name: birthdayCount3_four
mainTheorems.description: The main closed form for n = 4: the number of ways to seat four labelled people on d days with at most two per day is d⁴ − 4d² + 3d, stated over ℤ to avoid truncated-subtraction artefacts. Proved by casing on d ≤ 2 (decide, kernel reduction — no native_decide) and unfolding the recurrence for d ≥ 3 (simp on R_succ/R_one/R_zero, then push_cast and ring).
mainTheorems.leanType: (d : ℕ) → (birthdayCount3 4 d : ℤ) = d ^ 4 - 4 * d ^ 2 + 3 * d

mainTheorems.name: birthdayCount3_four_factored
mainTheorems.description: The factored form of the n = 4 count: d(d−1)(d²+d−3) over ℤ, obtained from birthdayCount3_four by ring. Exhibits the d and (d−1) factors (no valid seating uses fewer than the available days trivially) and the quadratic residual.

mainTheorems.name: birthdayCount3_four_eq_nat
mainTheorems.description: The closed form as a truncation-safe ℕ identity for d ≥ 1: birthdayCount3 4 d + 4d² = d⁴ + 3d. Moves the subtracted 4d² to the other side so the statement holds in ℕ without truncated subtraction; proved by zify and linarith from birthdayCount3_four.
mainTheorems.leanType: (d : ℕ) → (hd : 1 ≤ d) → birthdayCount3 4 d + 4 * d ^ 2 = d ^ 4 + 3 * d

mainTheorems.name: R_one
mainTheorems.description: One-step evaluation of the slot recurrence: R 1 e s = e + s, by simp. Base case reused when unfolding the n = 4 recurrence down to depth 1.
mainTheorems.leanType: (e s : ℕ) → R 1 e s = e + s

mainTheorems.name: R_succ
mainTheorems.description: The defining unfold of the slot recurrence (a @[simp] rfl-lemma): R (n+1) e s = e · R n (e-1) (s+1) + s · R n e (s-1), splitting on whether the next person takes a fresh day (e empty days) or pairs onto a singly-occupied day (s single days).
mainTheorems.leanType: (n e s : ℕ) → R (n + 1) e s = e * R n (e - 1) (s + 1) + s * R n e (s - 1)

mainTheorems.name: R_zero
mainTheorems.description: Base case of the slot recurrence (a @[simp] rfl-lemma): R 0 e s = 1 — the empty seating is the unique arrangement of zero people.

overview.historicalContext: The classical birthday problem — first analysed by Richard von Mises in 1939 and popularised through William Feller's probability text — asks for the probability of a coincidence among n people's birthdays. The 'k=3' (triple-coincidence) variant instead counts seatings of n people on d days with at most two per day, the configurations that avoid a triple collision; the parent entry built an O(n²) slot recurrence R(n,e,s) tracking the numbers of empty and singly-occupied days, and established the closed forms birthdayCount3 1 d = d, birthdayCount3 2 d = d², and birthdayCount3 3 d = d³ − d. The single-day case d = 1 recovers the involution / telephone numbers OEIS A000085 (arrangements into parts of size at most two), placing this count in a well-studied combinatorial lineage. The next term in the d-polynomial sequence, for n = 4, had not been recorded.
overview.problemStatement: Determine the exact closed form of birthdayCount3 4 d — the number of ways to seat four labelled people on d days with at most two per day — and prove it without native_decide.
overview.text: By the parent recurrence R 4 d 0 = d · R 3 (d−1) 1, and unfolding two further levels (using R 1 e s = e + s at the base), one obtains R 4 d 0 = d(d−1)(d²+d−3) = d⁴ − 4d² + 3d. We verify this directly: for d = 0, 1, 2 by evaluation, and for d = k+3 by unfolding the recurrence symbolically (the truncated subtractions d−1, d−2, d−3 become k+2, k+1, k once d ≥ 3) and matching polynomials with ring over ℤ. A sanity check: at d = 4 the formula gives 256 − 64 + 12 = 204 = R 4 4 0.
overview.proofStrategy: Case-split on d (small cases by decide; d = k+3 by unfolding R via its equation lemmas, normalizing the natural subtractions, casting to ℤ, and closing with ring); derive the factored and ℕ forms algebraically.
keyInsights: The count is a degree-4 polynomial in d, the next entry after d, d², d³ − d for n = 1, 2, 3.
Writing d = k + 3 makes all truncated subtractions exact, turning the recurrence unfolding into a polynomial identity ring can close.
Working over ℤ sidesteps the n = 1 truncation artefact that the factored form d(d−1)(d²+d−3) absorbs only by accident.

The whole sequence d, d², d³−d, d⁴−4d²+3d is generated by the exponential generating function (1 + x + x²/2)^d: each per-day factor 1 + x + x²/2 encodes 'zero, one, or two people that day', and birthdayCount3 n d = n! · [xⁿ] (1 + x + x²/2)^d. The recurrence unfolded here is exactly the convolution this product hides — so the ad-hoc closed forms are the coefficients of one clean generating function.

The small-case branch (d = 0, 1, 2) is discharged by `decide`, i.e. kernel reduction, not `native_decide`; combined with the symbolic `ring` argument for d ≥ 3 this keeps the entire result dependent only on propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. That axiom hygiene is what lets this entry legitimately claim 0 axioms, where several of the parent's tabulated values — evaluated via `native_decide` — carry the compiler-trusting Lean.ofReduceBool dependency.
prerequisites: The parent slot recurrence R and birthdayCount3
Casting to ℤ and polynomial normalization (ring)

conclusion.summary: birthdayCount3 4 d = d⁴ − 4d² + 3d = d(d−1)(d²+d−3), the next closed form after the parent's n = 1, 2, 3 cases, proved 0-axiom (no native_decide). 6 theorems, 2 definitions, 77 lines.
conclusion.implications: Continues the explicit closed-form sequence for the k=3 birthday count and demonstrates that these values are accessible by symbolic recurrence unfolding rather than the parent's native_decide evaluation, keeping the result axiom-free.
openQuestions: Find the general closed form birthdayCount3 n d as a polynomial in d (a signed sum over involutions / telephone-number structure) and prove it by induction on n.
Identify the exponential generating function ∑ birthdayCount3 n d · x^n / n! = (1 + x + x²/2)^d and derive the closed forms from it.
Extend to the k-way count R_k tracking a full multiplicity histogram, as in the parent's open questions.

This entry's exact n = 4 value d⁴ − 4d² + 3d is a concrete k = 3 evaluation of the count that framework tracks — it is the open question 'extend to the k-way count R_k' listed here, made explicit for one term.

Complementary view of the same k=3 count: that entry derives the large-n coincidence threshold n ≈ (6d²ln2)^(1/3), whereas this entry pins down the exact small-n closed form. Together they bracket birthdayCount3 from both the asymptotic and the exact-enumeration sides.
Grandparent: the k=3 extension-counting framework from which the parent slot recurrence R is built. This entry is a leaf computation within that framework, evaluating its count at n = 4.

The classical birthday problem at the root of this open-question chain. The k=3 'at most two per day' count refined here is the triple-coincidence analogue of the original all-distinct birthday count.
